name: Xylometazoline

lead: Xylometazoline is an over-the-counter nasal spray that shrinks swollen nasal tissue so breathing is easier. It has been sold since 1959.
People interested in facial redness note that it works by vasoconstriction, but its labeled use is nasal congestion.

paras: It activates alpha-adrenergic receptors on nasal blood vessels, narrowing them and reducing swelling.

Irritation, headache and nosebleed are reported. Use beyond about five to seven days is not advised because of rebound congestion. Check with a clinician if pregnant or if you have high blood pressure or heart conditions.

chain: Constricts blood vessels in the nasal lining
Clearer breathing; vasoconstriction is the property behind redness interest
angle.text: The nasal spray relieves congestion by shrinking nasal vessels. People interested in redness reduction point to the same vasoconstrictor action, though the labeled use is congestion.

lead: Xylometazoline is an imidazoline nasal decongestant sold over the counter as sprays and drops in many countries, with brand names such as Otrivin [1]. It narrows blood vessels in the nasal lining, which reduces swelling and opens the airway [2].

For appearance, its relevance is mainly through easier nasal breathing and the visibly paler look of the vasoconstricted nasal lining [1]. Interest in it for rosacea redness comes from the broader use of vasoconstrictors for facial flushing; the nasal product itself is labeled for congestion.
It was patented in 1956 and entered medical use in 1959 [1]. Studies have examined it for congestion, nosebleed prevention during intubation, sleep apnea with congestion and other settings.

paras: Labeled use is temporary relief of nasal congestion from colds, hay fever and sinusitis [1]. Hospital and clinic uses include pretreatment before nasal procedures [3][4].

Reported effects include nasal irritation, headache, nosebleed and trouble sleeping [1]. Use beyond about five days is not recommended because stopping can cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) [1]. A 2026 review found no rebound congestion in studies of up to 10 days of xylometazoline [5]. The US label advises asking a doctor if symptoms last over 7 days [6].
It is a direct alpha-adrenergic agonist acting on receptors in nasal blood vessels, causing local vasoconstriction [2][7].

A randomized trial in children found xylometazoline with lidocaine jelly reduced nosebleed after nasotracheal intubation (7.5% versus 27.5% with saline) [3]. A crossover trial in twelve people with sleep apnea and nasal congestion tested a week of xylometazoline against placebo [4]. A Cochrane review examined nasal decongestants for the common cold [8]. No published trial of xylometazoline for rosacea redness was found.
